The strongest surviving capability is adhesion that preserves a stored order while its contact spacings change

I have sustained the retained-order branch and given it a more demanding function: a surface should recognize the same ordered pattern after substantial redistribution of the distances between its sites, and retain a useful normal adhesion response while individual contacts remain able to release.

A common physical model now supports that operation conditionally. It includes finite contact geometry, competing and mismatched contacts, sliding entropy, unwanted depletion contacts at stops, and the mechanical path by which a support pulls a seated partner out.

The conventional comparison materially limits the result. A conventional linkage can reproduce the calculated response when given enough separately allocated travel. In the comparison below, the rail uses 12 μm of shared slack; the best numerical conventional design found needs about 29.1 μm of separately allocated travel to match its combined adhesion-work and discrimination targets. That is a distinction in a specified mechanical resource. Its value as a material depends on how economically each construction can supply that resource.

There is also a consequential failure: the four-contact example is thermally too weak to act as a robust force selector on its own, despite having separated correct-pattern and wrong-pattern force curves.

1. A physical contact that accommodates registration and release

I replaced the buried, tightly registered contact with an open spherical cup and a spherical key. Each cup sits on a carriage retained on a single capped guide. The carriages cannot pass one another, but their axial separations can change. The external keys sit on a facing support, with bounded transverse travel.

This separates four requirements in an actual mechanical construction:

Retention: captivity on the capped guide preserves the sequence of carriage types.
Sliding: the carriages redistribute the available axial space.
Registration: a sphere seats against a complementary spherical cavity; sphere orientation does not have to be selected.
Release: the sphere can withdraw through the open mouth while other contacts remain seated.

Each row uses one continuous guide. External bonds do not become part of the sliding path, so this version does not require a carriage to traverse an exchanging network junction.

The chemical ingredient has primary experimental support. Sacanna and colleagues demonstrated reversible, shape-selective colloidal binding through depletion attraction between spherical keys and particles with spherical cavities. Their results also establish an important correction: an oversized key can bind at a cavity rim. Geometric mismatch cannot simply be represented as a zero binding constant.

An earlier control optimized only for discrimination reached about a 14-fold worst-case preference, exceeding the rail’s roughly 10-fold preference. The external precedents further narrow the opportunity:

Reversible, sequence-sensitive molecular zippers and competitive displacement already exist in boronic-acid/catechol peptide systems.

Mobile ligands on capped polyrotaxanes already enhance multivalent recognition; mobility itself is established functionality.

Surface-force experiments already show that mobile membrane ligands can accommodate receptor geometry and strengthen adhesion.

Mobile DNA linkers have been directly observed recruiting into contacts and repeatedly exchanging while multivalent adhesion persists. Their exchange kinetics materially affect selectivity.

The distinctive question is therefore whether a useful construction can retain a programmed order and supply large, redistributable spacing freedom economically, with compatible contact turnover.

What the branch now supports

The useful result is a conditional construction for adhesion that preserves an address through substantial changes in spacing, together with a conventional device that reproduces its response after paying additional travel reserve. The strongest surviving capability is adhesion that preserves a stored order while its contact spacings change

I have sustained the retained-order branch and given it a more demanding function: a surface should recognize the same ordered pattern after substantial redistribution of the distances between its sites, and retain a useful normal adhesion response while individual contacts remain able to release.

A common physical model now supports that operation conditionally. It includes finite contact geometry, competing and mismatched contacts, sliding entropy, unwanted depletion contacts at stops, and the mechanical path by which a support pulls a seated partner out.

The conventional comparison materially limits the result. A conventional linkage can reproduce the calculated response when given enough separately allocated travel. In the comparison below, the rail uses 12 μm of shared slack; the best numerical conventional design found needs about 29.1 μm of separately allocated travel to match its combined adhesion-work and discrimination targets. That is a distinction in a specified mechanical resource. Its value as a material depends on how economically each construction can supply that resource.

There is also a consequential failure: the four-contact example is thermally too weak to act as a robust force selector on its own, despite having separated correct-pattern and wrong-pattern force curves.

1. A physical contact that accommodates registration and release

I replaced the buried, tightly registered contact with an open spherical cup and a spherical key. Each cup sits on a carriage retained on a single capped guide. The carriages cannot pass one another, but their axial separations can change. The external keys sit on a facing support, with bounded transverse travel.

This separates four requirements in an actual mechanical construction:

  • Retention: captivity on the capped guide preserves the sequence of carriage types.
  • Sliding: the carriages redistribute the available axial space.
  • Registration: a sphere seats against a complementary spherical cavity; sphere orientation does not have to be selected.
  • Release: the sphere can withdraw through the open mouth while other contacts remain seated.

Each row uses one continuous guide. External bonds do not become part of the sliding path, so this version does not require a carriage to traverse an exchanging network junction.

The chemical ingredient has primary experimental support. Sacanna and colleagues demonstrated reversible, shape-selective colloidal binding through depletion attraction between spherical keys and particles with spherical cavities. Their results also establish an important correction: an oversized key can bind at a cavity rim. Geometric mismatch cannot simply be represented as a zero binding constant. irvinelab.uchicago.edu

The calculation uses a specified hemispherical shell rather than treating those experimental particles as exact copies of the proposed geometry. Its potential is

U={+∞,hard overlap,−ΠVoverlap,otherwise,U= \begin{cases} +\infty,&\text{hard overlap},\\[2mm] -\Pi V_{\mathrm{overlap}},&\text{otherwise}, \end{cases}U=⎩⎨⎧​+∞,−ΠVoverlap​,​hard overlap,otherwise,​

where VoverlapV_{\mathrm{overlap}}Voverlap​ is the overlap of the depletant-exclusion volumes of the actual bodies. The same depletant acts on the cups, keys and modeled bearing or stop features. There are no separately assigned association energies or rupture thresholds.

A particular narrow rear mounting stem for the cup was checked separately and adds neither hard overlap nor additional key–stem depletion attraction in that range.

This is ordinary collective barrier amplification applied to the retained-order interface. Its relevance is the combined operation: preserving a load-bearing response across spacing distortions while distinguishing reordered targets.

A rigid support does not require an infinite stiffness. For example, an explicitly assumed E=2E=2E=2 GPa beam, 400 μm400\,\mu\mathrm m400μm long, 32 μm32\,\mu\mathrm m32μm wide and 10 μm10\,\mu\mathrm m10μm thick has a simple cantilever estimate of roughly 0.250.250.25 N/m stiffness. Two qualifications remain decisive. Individual contacts must equilibrate sufficiently during loading, and additional deformation modes must not provide an easier peeling or rotation path. The barrier calculation supplies neither a measured lifetime nor a kinetic prefactor.

4. The conventional alternative can recover the operation

The comparison must preserve order on both sides. A freely rearranging collection of ligands is too weak a sole comparator.

The principal numerical control therefore has the same contact heads, bath, transverse contact mechanism, valency and overall axial confinement, but neighboring addressed heads have separately limited travel:

0≤gi≤ci.0\le g_i\le c_i.0≤gi​≤ci​.

This represents a conventional chain of independently telescoping links or sufficiently compliant retained tethers. The numerical version has flat link free energy below each limit; it is an explicit mechanical idealization, not a claimed measured polymer force law.

I optimized the control for the joint target:

  1. maintain at least the rail’s worst correct/decoy discrimination;
  2. maximize its worst correct-target reversible separation work across the spacing layouts.

Why shared travel can help

For complete registration, each conventional link must accommodate whichever target gap appears at its own position. In this example the largest required free gap is 9.2 μm9.2\,\mu\mathrm m9.2μm. Accounting for the finite capture widths gives the necessary capacities

c1≥9.10,c2≥9.075,c3≥9.05  μmc_1\ge9.10,\qquad c_2\ge9.075,\qquad c_3\ge9.05\;\mu\mathrm mc1​≥9.10,c2​≥9.075,c3​≥9.05μm

to permit full registration in all three extreme layouts. Their sum is 27.225 μm27.225\,\mu\mathrm m27.225μm. Merely permitting that branch is weaker than supplying enough equilibrium weight to match the full response, which explains why the numerical parity point lies higher.

More generally, a mobile shared interval can redistribute one reserve among many gaps. A design with independent per-link limits must duplicate enough reserve at every location where the large gap could occur.

But travel length is not automatically material cost or occupied volume. Thin flexible contour may be cheap to store. A conventional reeling mechanism can also reproduce zero-cost redistribution over a fixed total span: identical constant-tension elements have

∑iUi(gi)=T0∑igi+constant,\sum_i U_i(g_i)=T_0\sum_i g_i+\mathrm{constant},i∑​Ui​(gi​)=T0​i∑​gi​+constant,

which is unchanged when the gaps redistribute at fixed total span. Real passive spooling and force plateaus have been demonstrated with synthetic filaments and droplets, although those demonstrations do not supply this aqueous colloidal device at the proposed scale. arxiv.org

The external precedents further narrow the opportunity:

  • Reversible, sequence-sensitive molecular zippers and competitive displacement already exist in boronic-acid/catechol peptide systems. PMC
  • Mobile ligands on capped polyrotaxanes already enhance multivalent recognition; mobility itself is established functionality. PubMed
  • Surface-force experiments already show that mobile membrane ligands can accommodate receptor geometry and strengthen adhesion. PMC
  • Mobile DNA linkers have been directly observed recruiting into contacts and repeatedly exchanging while multivalent adhesion persists. Their exchange kinetics materially affect selectivity. arxiv.org

The distinctive question is therefore whether a useful construction can retain a programmed order and supply large, redistributable spacing freedom economically, with compatible contact turnover.

What the branch now supports

The useful result is a conditional construction for adhesion that preserves an address through substantial changes in spacing, together with a conventional device that reproduces its response after paying additional travel reserve. The common-potential calculation has advanced the earlier interface obstruction: registration, finite capture, individual release, stop-mediated loading and full equilibrium weights now coexist in one specified model.

The remaining physical gap is the integrated guide and stage assembly. The stem clearances are established for the specified geometry, but the complete finite-clearance bearings, neighboring supports, rotational compliance and their state-dependent depletion interactions have not all been supplied. Published demonstrations of retained motion and reversible contacts do not establish that intersection. Real charge, roughness and polymer behavior also need to remain compatible with the modeled contact window.

This is therefore more specific than lacking experimental access: the complete accessible-surface Hamiltonian and the mobility of the assembled device are still unfinished material inputs. Assigning exchange rates would conceal that gap.

I would sustain the branch around this resource question: whether a realizable retained guide can supply the shared travel, contact turnover and normal-force response more effectively than the conventional linkage with roughly 29 μm29\,\mu\mathrm m29μm of separate reserve.
